citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
A six-year-old male Yorkshire Terrier (603-891-084) “Prince Parti” had a left foot open lesion. The lesion was weeping,
reddened, and appeared irritated. The hair around the lesion was darkened and wet. The licensee was aware of the
lesion and was putting “nustock” on the wound. The licensee doesn’t have a protocol for treating lesions in their Program
of Vet Care (PVC) nor has the licensee contacted their attending veterinarian (AV). Facilities must have direct and
frequent communication with their veterinarian. The licensee must correct by contacting their veterinarian.
A female Yorkshire Terrier (605-797-068) has a three-inch-long laceration on her right hip. The licensee stated they
contacted their AV by text message on August 9, 2026, but didn’t receive a reply. The licensee didn’t contact or speak
with any other veterinarian. The licensee stated they sutured the laceration themselves on August 9th and the dog must
have chewed out the sutures. The laceration appears reddened and the dog appears unusually subdued. The licensee
doesn’t have a protocol for treating lacerations in their PVC. Facilities must have direct and frequent communication with
their veterinarian. The licensee must correct by contacting their AV.
Correct by 13 August 2026

citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
A 6-week-old male Yorkshire Terrier born to dam Julia (605-787-675) has a clouded right eye. The cloudy eye appeared
raised. Eye issues can be painful and result in vision loss. The licensee was unaware of the issue and hadn’t contacted
their AV. Daily observations are required for all animals to assess their health and well-being. The licensee must observe
all animals daily and have the puppy seen by their AV.
Correct by August 13, 2026

17 adult dogs are housed in primary enclosures where the exterior portion of the enclosures aren’t connected to the wall
of the enclosure building. This leaves gaps ranging from 3”-4”. The gaps put the dogs at risk for entrapment,
entanglement, and falling approximately five feet to the ground. Primary enclosures must be maintained in good repair.
The facility must repair the primary enclosure, so the exterior portion of the suspended enclosure is reconnected to the
enclosure building.
The interior flooring of a primary enclosure housing two Yorkshire Terriers has disconnected from the building frame in the
adult dog building. APHIS officials watched pinch point type gaps created as the flooring separated under the dog’s
weight. Primary enclosures must be maintained in good repair. The facility must repair the primary enclosure floor.
Correct by September 26, 2026

Two primary enclosures housing 6 puppies and 5 puppies respectively have floors constructed in a manner that allowed
their feet to become entrapped and their legs stuck. APHIS officials observed numerous puppies with their legs through
the flooring at the time of inspection.
Numerous holes ranging from approximately 3” to 4” in diameter were seen in the flooring throughout multiple enclosures.
Flooring must be constructed and maintained in a manner that protects the dogs’ legs from injury and does not allow feet
to pass through the flooring.
The licensee must construct and maintain primary enclosures and flooring to protect the dogs’ legs from injury and
prevent them from passing through the floor.
One primary enclosure housing two Dachshunds had sharp points from the broken enclosure wire. Sharp points can
cause injury to dogs. Primary enclosures must be constructed and maintained so that they don’t have any sharp points to
protect the dogs from injury.
Correct by September 26, 2026
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with licensee.
Additional Inspectors:
Michael Tygart, VETERINARY MEDICAL OFFICER n
